name: MathlibAnnex.BilipschitzOrientation.integral_det_fderiv_eq_signed_volume
title: The signed Jacobian integral is a sign times target volume

content.display_title: The signed Jacobian integral is a sign times target volume
content.one_sentence_role: Uses preconnectedness to obtain a constant, positive measure to identify its sign, and finite measure to integrate it.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $E=\mathbb R^n$ have the sup norm $\|\cdot\|_\infty$. Let $S,T\subseteq E$ be open, and let $f,g:E\to E$ be globally Lipschitz maps whose restrictions $f|_S:S\to T$ and $g|_T:T\to S$ are mutually inverse. Fix a number $\ell>0$ such that
$$\ell\|x-x'\|_\infty\le\|f(x)-f(x')\|_\infty\qquad(x,x'\in E).$$

Assume that $T$ is preconnected (it has no separation into two nonempty relatively open subsets) and that its Lebesgue measure $\lambda(T)$ satisfies $0<\lambda(T)<\infty$.

Write $Df(x):E\to E$ for the Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$ when it exists, and set $Df(x)=0$ at other points. Define the signed Jacobian by $J_f(x)=\det Df(x)$. Then there exists $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}$ such that
$$\int_S J_f(x)\,d\lambda(x)=\varepsilon\lambda(T).$$
Here the finite measure $\lambda(T)$ is identified with its real value, so this is an equality of real numbers.
content.assumptions:
The target $T$ is **preconnected**, has **positive** Lebesgue measure, and has **finite** Lebesgue measure:
$$T\text{ is preconnected},\qquad 0<\lambda(T)<\infty.$$
These conditions are additional to openness and the following inverse and global metric assumptions.

The sets $S,T\subseteq E$ are open. The inverse and image conditions are
$$\begin{aligned}
f(S)&\subseteq T,&g(T)&\subseteq S,\\
g(f(x))&=x\quad(x\in S),&f(g(y))&=y\quad(y\in T).
\end{aligned}$$
The global bounds use specified constants $C_f,C_g\ge0$ and $\ell>0$:
$$\ell\|x-x'\|_\infty\le\|f(x)-f(x')\|_\infty\le C_f\|x-x'\|_\infty\qquad(x,x'\in E),$$
$$\|g(y)-g(y')\|_\infty\le C_g\|y-y'\|_\infty\qquad(y,y'\in E).$$
The estimates hold on all of $E$, not just on $S$ or $T$. The inverse identities are required only on $S$ and $T$.
content.conclusion: The integral of the signed Jacobian is either $\lambda(T)$ or $-\lambda(T)$. The sign $\varepsilon$ is obtained from the maps; it is not fixed in advance.
content.proof_summary: Identify the almost-everywhere constant value of the transported sign at a point outside its null exceptional set. Then substitute the constant function $1$ into signed transfer.

proof_steps.text:
**Obtain a constant and identify its value.** Define
$$s_f(x)=\begin{cases}1,&J_f(x)\ge0,\\-1,&J_f(x)<0,\end{cases}\qquad\sigma_f(y)=s_f(g(y)).$$
By [constancy of the transported sign](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Calculus/BilipschitzOrientation/Constancy.lean#L50-L56), applied with the assumed preconnectedness of $T$, there is $c\in\mathbb R$ for which the set
$$N_c=\{y\in T:\sigma_f(y)\ne c\}$$
satisfies $\lambda(N_c)=0$. Since $\lambda(T)>0$, choose $y_0\in T\setminus N_c$. Then
$$c=\sigma_f(y_0)\in\{-1,1\}.$$
This is [the positive-measure sign-identification lemma](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Calculus/BilipschitzOrientation/Constancy.lean#L58-L70) with the same almost-everywhere equality and the hypothesis $\lambda(T)>0$. Put $\varepsilon=c$.

**Integrate using finite target measure.** The relevant integrability calculation is
$$\int_T|1|\,d\lambda=\lambda(T)<\infty.$$
Thus the observable $\phi(y)=1$ satisfies the hypothesis of [signed transfer](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Calculus/BilipschitzOrientation/Basic.lean#L205-L280). With the same maps and sets, that formula and Step 1 give
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_S J_f(x)\,d\lambda(x)
&=\int_T\sigma_f(y)\,d\lambda(y)\\
&=\int_T c\,d\lambda(y)=c\lambda(T)=\varepsilon\lambda(T).
\end{aligned}$$
The replacement of $\sigma_f$ by $c$ uses $\lambda(N_c)=0$. The final integral is finite because $T$ has finite measure.

content.lean_realization_notes: The proof uses the three target hypotheses at different stages: preconnectedness gives an almost-everywhere constant, positive measure identifies its value as a sign, and finite measure permits integration of that constant.
